**`src/index.js`**
- `createMcpHandler` is imported from `agents/mcp/server`. That's the stateless handler that takes a factory function, so no Durable Object is involved. In agents 0.27, the other forms are marked deprecated: passing an old SDK v1 `McpServer` to `createMcpHandler`, and `experimental_createMcpHandler`.
- The factory builds a fresh `McpServer` (from the v2 `@modelcontextprotocol/server` package) for each request. It registers `add` with `inputSchema: z.object({ a: z.number(), b: z.number() })` and returns `{ content: [{ type: 'text', text: String(a + b) }] }`.
- The Worker's `fetch` sends a request to the MCP handler only when the path is exactly `/mcp`. Every other path still goes through `routeAgentRequest`, and the 404 fallback is unchanged. `fetch` now also takes `ctx`, which the handler needs.

**`package.json`**
- Added `@modelcontextprotocol/server` at `2.0.0`, the version agents 0.27.0 pins, and `zod` at `^4.6.5`. Both were already in `node_modules` as dependencies of agents, so no install is needed.

The quickest test is `npm run dev`, then send a JSON-RPC `tools/call` for `add` with `{"a":2,"b":3}` to `http://localhost:8787/mcp`. The answer should be the text `5`.

`wrangler.jsonc` has no `nodejs_compat` compatibility flag, and the agents package imports `node:async_hooks`. That was already the case before my change. If `wrangler dev` reports that it can't resolve Node built-ins, add `"compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"]`.

I added tracing to the AI SDK call in `src/summarize.js` and enabled traces in `wrangler.jsonc`. Nothing has been run or built: `ai` and `workers-ai-provider` aren't in `node_modules`, so I couldn't test it. Run `npm install` first.

**`src/summarize.js`**
- It now uses `wrapAISDK` from `agents/observability/ai`, the integration documented in agents 0.27.0, which supports AI SDK v6 and v7. It imports `ai` as a namespace and pulls `generateText` from the wrapped copy.
- Each call should show up as an `invoke_agent summarizer` span with a `chat {model}` child span for the Workers AI request. Token counts, provider and response model are attached to the spans.
- I added `telemetry: { functionId: 'summarizer' }` because v7 uses that value as the agent name on the spans. The docs say it should be a fixed logical name, not a request, user or session ID. Rename it if you prefer something else.
- Prompts and outputs are not recorded by default. Pass `wrapAISDK(ai, { storeMessages: true })` if you want the message content on the spans.
- On v7 you don't need to register a separate telemetry integration; the wrapper is enough.

**`wrangler.jsonc`**
- Added `"observability": { "traces": { "enabled": true } }`. Without it the wrapper does nothing, because the runtime has no tracing turned on.

The spans should appear in Workers Observability after you deploy.

I've added tracing to the AI SDK call in `src/summarize.js` and turned on traces in `wrangler.jsonc`. I haven't run or deployed it: `ai` and `workers-ai-provider` are in `package.json` but not in `node_modules` or `package-lock.json`, so the Worker won't build until you run `npm install`.

**`src/summarize.js`**

- Each call creates an `invoke_agent` span, plus a child span per model request named `chat @cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast`. The spans carry the model, Workers AI as provider, token usage, finish reason and the AI Gateway log ID when there is one.

**`wrangler.jsonc`**
- **`"observability": { "enabled": true, "traces": { "enabled": true } }`**: without this, Workers Observability doesn't collect the spans.
- **`"compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"]`**: the agents tracer imports `node:async_hooks`. Your existing `Agent` code probably needs this flag too.

Optional settings:
- **Prompt and response text:** spans don't include them by default. Use `wrapAISDK(ai, { storeMessages: true })` to record them (`storeTools: true` does the same for tool calls). They're off by default because they can put user data into your traces.
- **Span name:** the top-level span is just `invoke_agent` unless the call has a name. In v7, passing `telemetry: { functionId: 'summarize' }` to `generateText` should rename it to `invoke_agent summarize`. I left it out because I couldn't check v7's types without `ai` installed.

The chat now re-renders on every streamed chunk instead of in batches. I haven't run the app, so I haven't watched it render per chunk or checked the meter's numbers.

**Cause:** `useAgentChat` (from the `agents` package) throttles chat updates to 50 ms by default. When chunks arrived faster than that, several were combined into one re-render, so `TokenMeter` counted fewer chunks than really came in.

**Fix:** In `src/client/Chat.jsx:8` I changed the call to `useAgentChat({ agent, throttle: false })`. The package's own type docs say passing `false` makes it render every chunk as it arrives. In the package code, `false` means no throttle value is passed on to the underlying chat hook, so updates aren't delayed.

Rendering on every chunk means more re-renders while a reply streams. That's the behaviour you asked for, but it could cost some performance on very fast streams or long message lists.

The chat now re-renders on every streamed chunk instead of in batches. I haven't run the app to watch it happen.

**Cause:** `useAgentChat` (from `agents/chat/react`) groups state updates into 50ms windows by default. So when chunks arrived quickly, several of them shared one re-render, and the TokenMeter undercounted.

**Fix:** in `src/client/Chat.jsx:8` I passed `throttle: false`. The library's type definitions say that setting means "render every chunk as it arrives." It also correctly handles both spellings of the option that `@ai-sdk/react` uses across its versions.

One caveat: React can still merge updates that happen in the same browser task. I expect that's fine here, because each WebSocket message is handled as its own task.

I changed one line in `src/client/Chat.jsx:8`, so the chat now updates on every streamed chunk as it arrives. I haven't run the app to watch it happen.

```jsx
const { messages, sendMessage, status } = useAgentChat({ agent, throttle: false });
```

**What was wrong:** the installed `agents` package delays chat updates by 50 ms by default and groups any chunks that arrive within that window into one update. That meant `TokenMeter` saw several chunks as a single re-render, so its tokens/s reading came out too low.

**The fix:** `throttle: false` turns that delay off. Per the package's own docs in `node_modules/agents/dist/chat/react.d.ts`, this makes it "render every chunk as it arrives." The package sets the option under both the old and new names for you, so this works with either version of the AI SDK that it supports.

One limit: if two chunks arrive in the same browser event (for example, packed into one WebSocket message), React still merges them into one render. Chunks that arrive as separate messages each get their own render.

I made the change in `src/counter.js`, but I haven't bundled or run it: the `wrangler deploy --dry-run` check was blocked by permission prompts, so nothing is tested yet.

**What changed**
- **Scheduling:** `Counter` still extends `DurableObject`, not `Agent`. It now uses the package's `Scheduler`, attached through `Lifecycle.install(this).use(this.scheduler)`. The scheduler has one callback, `compact`, which calls `this.compact()`.
- **Registration:** `onStart()` registers the cron schedule `0 3 * * *`. The schedule is saved in the object's SQLite storage, so it survives restarts. Cron schedules are deduplicated by default, so registering it again on every start doesn't create duplicates.
- **Start-up on RPC calls:** calls from other Workers skip the lifecycle's automatic start-up, so `hit()` and `count()` now begin with `await this.lifecycle.start()`. Without that, an object that is only ever called over RPC would never register the schedule.
- **No hand-written `alarm()`:** `Lifecycle.install` provides `alarm()` (and `fetch`) itself. Adding your own `alarm()` to `Counter` later would break the schedule; I left a comment saying so.

**Things to know**
- **Experimental API:** the package docs mark `Scheduler` and `agents/lifecycle` as experimental and say they may change between releases. You pin `agents` to exactly `0.27.0`, so check this code when you upgrade.
- **Timezone:** the cron time is worked out with the runtime's local time, and Workers run in UTC, so it fires at 03:00 UTC.
- **Only objects that have been called get the schedule:** a `Counter` instance registers it the first time it's called. One that has never been called has nothing to compact anyway.
- **Startup timeout:** the docs say an RPC call that arrives before startup must use `start()`/`ready()`, or startup can intermittently time out. That's why both RPC methods call `start()` first. If you add more RPC methods that touch storage or the scheduler, start them the same way.

To check it, run `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run` to confirm it bundles. Then call `hit()` on an object and look for a pending cron entry in that object's schedules.

I've changed `src/counter.js` so Counter runs `compact()` every day at 03:00 UTC, using the agents package's scheduler. I haven't built or run it: the attempt to run `wrangler deploy --dry-run` was blocked by the permission check, and there are no tests.

**How it works:**
- Counter is still a plain Durable Object. It now sets up two helpers from the agents package: a scheduler (from `agents/schedules`) with `compact` registered as its job, and a lifecycle helper (from `agents/lifecycle`). The lifecycle helper adds Counter's `alarm()` handler for you, so there is no hand-written alarm code.
- When Counter starts up, it registers the cron `'0 3 * * *'` for `compact()`. The schedule is saved in the object's own SQLite storage. Repeating the same cron setup doesn't create duplicates, so it's safe for this to run every time Counter wakes up.

**Things to check:**
1. **The schedule is only created when `hit()` or `count()` is called.** Calls from other Workers skip the lifecycle's automatic startup, so both methods now start it explicitly. Until a Counter instance gets its first `hit()` or `count()` after this deploys, it has no schedule. After that, the schedule is stored and the daily runs keep themselves going.
2. **Callers must look Counter up by name.** Startup needs the object's name. It works with `env.Counter.getByName(...)` or `idFromName(...)`. With `newUniqueId()` or `idFromString()`, `hit()` and `count()` will throw. I couldn't see the calling Workers, so please confirm how they look Counter up.
3. **New behaviour:** Counter now answers plain HTTP requests (`fetch`) with a 404. This has no effect on RPC calls.
4. **Experimental API:** the agents docs mark the scheduler and lifecycle helpers used here as experimental, so they may change between releases. You're pinned to `agents@0.27.0`, so check this when you upgrade.

To check the build yourself, run `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run`.

I've wired ToolGateway (`src/gateway.js`) up to the MCP server, but I haven't built or run it. My dry-run bundle (`wrangler deploy --dry-run`) needed your approval and didn't run, so nothing has been tested.

**What changed**
- ToolGateway is still a plain `DurableObject`. I didn't change `index.js` or `wrangler.jsonc`.
- It creates an `MCPClientManager` and attaches it with `Lifecycle.install(this).use(this.mcp)`. The agents package docs (`docs/mcp-client.md`) show this pattern for a plain Durable Object. They also mark using the manager outside an Agent as experimental.
- **Saved across eviction:** the manager stores the server as a row in the object's SQLite storage. When the object wakes up, the lifecycle start step reconnects it. Your `v2` migration already declares ToolGateway as `new_sqlite_classes`, so that storage exists.
- **`listTools()`:**
  1. It starts the lifecycle first. Calls from other Workers go over RPC and skip `fetch`, so nothing else would trigger the reconnect.
  2. It makes sure the server is set up under the fixed id `tools`. If it's already saved, it waits up to 30s for the reconnect and stops there if the connection is ready.
  3. Otherwise it registers the server if needed, connects, loads the tool list, and throws if connecting or loading fails.
  4. It returns `this.mcp.listTools()`.
- **Concurrent calls** share one setup, so the server isn't registered twice.
- **If `TOOLS_MCP_URL` changes**, the old saved server is removed and the new URL is registered.

**Limitations**
- **Login:** this assumes the server doesn't need OAuth. If it does, `listTools()` will throw, because no callback URL is set up.
- **Return format:** each tool includes a `serverId` field (always `"tools"`) alongside the fields the server sends. Strip it if your callers want the raw tool definitions.
- **Status names:** the package doesn't export its connection-status constants, so I compared against the plain values `'ready'` and `'connected'` instead.

To check it, run `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run` and then `wrangler dev` against a real MCP server.
